name: Cassia obtusifolia seed extract
lead: Cassia obtusifolia seed extract comes from the seeds of Senna obtusifolia (sicklepod), a legume used in East Asian traditional medicine, where the seeds are called jue ming zi in Chinese [1]. It appears in skincare as a soothing botanical ingredient, which is how it ties into looking better: calmer, more comfortable skin.
The seeds are traditionally roasted into a tea believed to benefit the eyes and to act as a laxative [1].

Laboratory research on the plant's compounds, such as the anthraquinone obtusifolin, has examined anti-inflammatory effects in mouse and liver models; these are not studies of the cosmetic extract on human skin.[2]

angle.text: Used in cosmetic formulas as a soothing botanical so skin looks and feels calmer. Traditional use centers on the seeds as tea.

paras: The plant grows across the Americas, Asia, Africa and Oceania and is often confused with Senna tora [1]. Seeds are also processed into cassia gum, a food thickener, and roasted as a coffee substitute [1].

No studies found of the cosmetic extract on human skin. Related lab and animal research includes a mouse osteoarthritis study of obtusifolin, an anthraquinone extracted from Senna obtusifolia, reporting reduced inflammation, and a 2026 study of obtusifolin in a liver inflammation model; neither tests skincare use.[2]

The plant is toxic to livestock eaten in larger amounts, causing muscle damage [1]. Human safety data on the cosmetic extract were not found; Wikipedia advises consulting a healthcare professional before using seeds or tea [1].

card.summary: A soothing botanical seed extract from sicklepod, used in skincare to leave skin looking calmer.

quick.overview:
Cassia obtusifolia seed extract comes from the sicklepod plant, whose seeds are used in East Asian traditional medicine.

In cosmetics it is included as a soothing botanical.
quick.mechanism: Skincare formulas include it for its soothing role. No studies of the cosmetic extract were found.
quick.risks: Human safety data are limited. The plant is toxic to livestock in large amounts.
